analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and off Florida.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit the Interior Department from leasing any part of the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, or Straits of Florida planning areas for oil, gas, or mineral exploration or production [S2][S3]. That would keep drilling rigs and the risk of spills out of waters off New Jersey, the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida, and New England. It was introduced in May 2017, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never received any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, beachgoers, and the tourism and fishing economies of Atlantic and Florida coastal states, which would be protected from oil spills and drilling infrastructure. Studies of spill impacts generally find that a single major spill can shut down fishing and depress tourism for years.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2][S3].
The prohibition is permanent and written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so it could not be reversed by a future administration's leasing plan without new legislation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to potential Atlantic and Straits of Florida reserves; the federal government forgoes any leasing revenue, and the nation forgoes some domestic energy production.

drawbacks.text: Blocking Atlantic leasing forgoes domestic energy production and any federal leasing revenue from those areas, and could leave the country more reliant on oil produced elsewhere or imported [S2].
The ban covers large planning areas where resource potential is not fully mapped, so it rules out exploration that could have revealed commercially significant deposits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is between protecting coastal economies and environments from spill risk against forgoing potential domestic energy supplies and revenue. For states whose beaches and fisheries drive large shares of their economies, protection outweighs speculative leasing gains, which is why every coastal-state Democratic senator present signed on; oil-producing-state senators saw it differently, and the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Menendez introduced the bill on May 1, 2017, joined by 15 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5].
The bill accumulated 19 cosponsors (18 Democrats and 1 independent) but received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote in the Senate [S4][S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record after the May 1 referral, and the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off: Atlantic and Florida waters remained legally available for future leasing, while coastal communities got no statutory protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and drilling access

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the committee chair, the bill never moved [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar leasing in four Atlantic and Florida planning areas, eliminating future drilling opportunities there. Drilling carries spill risk that coastal tourism and fishing economies would bear, so the industry's gain in access runs against coastal residents' interests.
A permanent ban would protect beaches and coastal economies from drilling activity and spill risk, the basis for the bill's name.
Fishing grounds along the Atlantic and off Florida would be shielded from seismic surveys, rig construction, and spill contamination.
